newsitem.title: USA: Tornado experts compare Texas storms to dynamite.
newsitem.headline: Tornado experts compare Texas storms to dynamite.

text.p: A convergence of warm, muggy air and a passing cold front as common in Texas as wildflowers in the spring ignited a tornado that devastated this central Texas town, meteorologists said on Wednesday.

A team from the National Weather Service assessing damage from the twister here estimated it packed winds of more than 200 miles an hour when it touched down in this small town about 40 miles (62 km) north of Austin, meteorologists said.

The twister was one of at least six reported across central Texas as the slow-moving cold front collided with a pocket of low pressure air saturated with moisture -- spring's recipe for violent storms and tornadoes in the southwest.

"Yesterday was one of the most volatile air masses we've seen in some time. It was like a stick of dynamite, all it needed was a spark to set it off," National Weather Service lead forecaster Mark Brundrett said.
At least 29 people died in central Texas and the death toll was expected to rise as rescue workers scoured the rubble of a rural Jarrell neighborhood leveled by the spring storms.

In Tuesday's storms, the first tornado was spotted south of Waco at about 1:20 p.m. CDT (2:20 p.m. EDT) (1820 GMT). As the line of storms began roaring down the Interstate 35 corridor, a twister smashed a house near Moody about 20 miles (32 km) south of Waco.
A second cell of storms soon formed and 35 minutes before the twister touched down in Jarrell, meteorologists issued a tornado warning for residents in the area.
"We actually saw it on the radar," Brundrett said.

In meteorological terms, the Jarrell twister could well be categorized as a rare F-4 storm -- a devastating tornado generating winds of 207-260 miles an hour capable of pulling up roadways, meteorologists said.

In human terms, the tornado is expected to rank as one of the deadliest on record in Texas. In May 1953, 114 people died when a twister devastated Waco. More recently, 42 were killed and more than 3,000 homes destroyed by an April 1979 twister that struck Wichita Falls.
